report:
Scientific evidence indicates that the claim is **generally true**, though its benefits depend heavily on environmental context.

Controlled research demonstrates that opening a bedroom door or window improves ventilation and prevents carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) accumulation during sleep. Landmark studies by Strøm-Tejsen et al. and recent trials at the Technical University of Denmark found that lower indoor $\text{CO}_2$ levels directly correlate with fewer night awakenings, deeper sleep, and improved next-day cognitive performance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/, https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day). Similarly, studies on open doors or windows show increased sleep efficiency due to better airflow (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed).

However, the view that opening a window *always* improves sleep quality is incorrect, as external factors can counteract the benefits of fresh air:

* **Noise pollution:** Outdoor traffic or neighborhood noise causes sleep fragmentation and micro-arousals.
* **Allergens and pollution:** Outdoor particulate matter, smog, or seasonal pollen can aggravate allergies and respiratory issues.
* **Thermal discomfort:** Drafts or extreme outdoor temperatures interfere with body temperature regulation, disrupting sleep stages (https://molekule.com/en-ca/blogs/all/sleep-window-open-night).

**Conclusion:** Opening a door or window reliably improves sleep quality by decreasing $\text{CO}_2$ concentration, provided external conditions (noise, pollution, and temperature) are favorable. If outdoor conditions are unfavorable, opening an internal door rather than a window provides ventilation benefits without external disruptions.
